seoTitle: How to Renew a Hostinger Domain and Its Pricing
metaDescription: Learn how to check your Hostinger domain expiry, renew active or expired domains, and understand renewal pricing, grace periods, and redemption fees.
intro: A domain that quietly expires can take your whole site offline, and the renewal price you actually pay is rarely the number you first see advertised. This guide walks through the Hostinger dashboard the way the video does: starting from the account home screen, checking what's registered under Domains, and following a renewal through to the checkout page where the real costs — billing period, ICANN fee, tax — show up. If you've only ever seen the flashy "$0.99 domain" banner, the order summary here is the more useful screen to understand.

steps.heading: Start from your Hostinger account home
steps.body: Everything begins at the hPanel home screen after you log in. The left-hand sidebar lists Websites, Domains, Horizons, Emails, VPS, and Billing, with a "Your to-dos" panel up top that flags anything needing attention, including services close to expiring. The Hosting widget on this page shows each plan's status and expiry date directly — in the video's account, a Cloud Startup plan is listed with its renewal date right next to the Manage button. This is the fastest place to notice an upcoming expiry before it becomes a problem, since Hostinger surfaces it without you having to dig into a separate billing page.

image.caption: The hPanel home screen. Active plans and their expiry dates show up directly in the Hosting widget, with Domains and Billing one click away in the sidebar.

steps.heading: Open Domains to see what's registered
steps.body: Click Domains in the sidebar and then Domain portfolio to see every domain tied to the account in one list, alongside options to get a new domain or transfer one in. This is also where an existing domain's renewal status and expiry countdown would normally appear once it's registered here. If the account has no domains registered directly — as in this example, where the portfolio is empty and only external domains are listed separately — you'll need to either register through Hostinger or manage the renewal from wherever the domain actually lives. Knowing this distinction matters, because a domain bought elsewhere and just pointed at Hostinger hosting won't renew from this screen at all.

image.caption: The Domain portfolio page. An empty portfolio like this one means no domains are registered directly through Hostinger — renewals for those would happen through the original registrar instead.

steps.heading: Choose a billing period at checkout
steps.body: Whether you're renewing an existing domain or registering one to bring it under Hostinger's management, the checkout screen is where the real pricing lives. It presents three billing periods side by side — typically 1, 2, and 3 years — each showing a struck-through list price next to the actual discounted rate you'll pay for that term. Longer terms usually carry a lower effective yearly rate, which is worth comparing before you commit, especially if you're renewing a domain you plan to keep for years anyway. A toggle for free WHOIS/domain privacy protection sits just below the term selector and is worth leaving on by default.

image.caption: The billing period selector at checkout, showing 1, 2, and 3-year options with the discounted rate next to the crossed-out list price.

steps.heading: Review the full order summary before paying
steps.body: The final payment screen is where the advertised price and the actual price reconcile. The Order Summary panel on the right itemizes the domain charge for the billing period you picked, WHOIS privacy protection (commonly free), a separate ICANN fee that's billed annually regardless of your term length, and applicable tax — GST in this example — before landing on a total. This breakdown is exactly what to screenshot or note if you're budgeting renewal costs for multiple domains, since the ICANN fee and tax are easy to forget when comparing headline renewal prices between registrars.

image.caption: The payment screen. The Order Summary breaks the total into the domain charge, WHOIS privacy protection, the annual ICANN fee, and tax.

steps.heading: Understand grace periods for expired domains
steps.body: If a domain has already lapsed rather than being renewed in time, it typically doesn't disappear immediately — most registrars, Hostinger included, hold it in a grace period during which you can still renew at the normal price. Miss that window and the domain can move into a redemption period, where getting it back usually costs significantly more than a standard renewal, on top of the renewal fee itself. Acting inside the grace period is the difference between a routine renewal and an expensive recovery, so treat any expiry warning email as a deadline rather than a suggestion.

faq.question: What happens if my Hostinger domain expires?
faq.answer: It usually enters a grace period during which you can still renew it at the normal price. If you miss that window too, it can move into a redemption period where getting it back costs noticeably more.

faq.question: Can I renew a domain before it expires?
faq.answer: Yes — renewing early through Domains → Domain portfolio avoids any service interruption and locks in whatever billing period and rate is being offered at the time.

faq.question: Why does the total at checkout look higher than the advertised price?
faq.answer: The order summary adds a separate annual ICANN fee and applicable tax on top of the domain charge itself, which the headline renewal price usually doesn't include.

faq.question: Does a longer billing term reduce the renewal price?
faq.answer: Often yes — 2-year and 3-year terms tend to show a lower effective yearly rate than a single 1-year renewal, so it's worth comparing all three options before paying.

faq.question: What if my domain isn't listed in Hostinger's Domain portfolio?
faq.answer: That means it's registered elsewhere and only connected to Hostinger for hosting. You'll need to manage its renewal through whichever registrar actually holds it, not through hPanel.
